newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Audi and Volkswagen announce Brazil $750 mln plant.
newsitem.headline: Audi and Volkswagen announce Brazil $750 mln plant.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Audi AG and its parent company Volkswagen unveiled Tuesday plans for a $750 million plant they will share in Brazil, the latest in a flurry of auto investments in the giant South American nation.
"We are sure that Brazil is now mature enough for a luxury mark in the car market," Audi President Herbert Demel said after meeting with Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

Construction of the plant in southern Parana state will begin early next year. Once completed in 1999 it will produce annually 30,000 units of Audi's new small car, the A3, and a similar number of Volkwagen's as yet unreleased Vento model, a planned successor to the Passat car.

The Brazilian market was expected to absorb 25,000 of the A3s each year with the remaining 5,000 earmarked for export to other countries in Latin America, a statement produced by the two companies said.
Audi and Volkswagen will pump about $250 million each into the new factory, which will be managed by Audi. A further $250 million expected to come from suppliers.

Audi cars are currently only available as imports in Brazil. The new plant represents Volkswagen's third assembly line in the country and is included in its $3 billion investment budget earmarked for Brazil between 1995 and 2000.

Pierre-Alain de Smedt, president of Volkswagen do Brasil, said the company would announce next year plans to expand its bus and truck plant opened this year in Resende, Rio de Janeiro state, possbily to produce the Caravelle line of vans.
The Parana plant might also be expanded in the future to produce other VW models, he said.

Demel attributed the choice of Parana to several factors including the sheer size of Brazil's market, which has nearly doubled since 1992 to 1.8 million units a year, easy access to Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, Brazil's partners in the Mercosur customs union, and a new climate of low inflation.
Brazil's controversial Car Industry Regime also played a part, he said.

The regime, which is currently being challenged at the World Trade Organisation, allows companies that manufacture locally and observe a 60 percent national content rule to import vehicles under a 35 percent tariff, half the normal rate.

The Audi-Volkswagen announcement follows last week's unveiling by General Motors of a $1.25 billion plan for three new plants in Brazil. GM also cited Brazil's car regime as a decisive factor in its decision to invest in the country.

Ford and Fiat also have announced plans to expand their existing output in Brazil while there has been no shortage of newcomers to Latin America's biggest market, led by Renault, Toyota, Mercedes Benz and Asia Motors.
Auto investment in Brazil is expected to reach about $19 billion between now and the year 2000.
